title: AI credit scoring: the tools, the rules and what to build first
description: Every library, platform and dataset a lender can use to score loans with AI, checked against US and EU rules, plus three builds and our pick.
summary: AI credit scoring predicts whether an applicant will repay, then has to say why in plain words when it says no. The model is the easy part. The decline reasons, the bias checks and the paperwork your examiner will ask for are what make or break it.
verdict: Start with a scorecard you can explain line by line: a weight-of-evidence scorecard in optbinning, or an Explainable Boosting Machine in interpret. Both give exact decline reasons, which US law requires. Move to LightGBM or XGBoost with SHAP only when your own benchmark shows the lift and you have a team to validate it. Use large language models to read documents, not to score: in published tests they lose to gradient boosting on credit data.

pickElse: No data science team: look at a platform such as Zest AI, Provenir, Taktile or Scienaptic. None publish prices; expect a contract.
Many thin-file applicants with little credit history: add bank-account cash-flow data from Plaid Check, Prism Data or Nova Credit before you change the model.
Most of the work is reading documents: spend on extraction first (recipe 3 below). The score is the easy part.
A small loan book: benchmark TabPFN against the scorecard. It did best on small, unbalanced default data in one 2026 study, but its newest weights need a paid licence for production.

ownData.intro: We pulled the latest release date, licence and monthly downloads for every open-source library a lender would use. Downloads show what teams actually run. Release dates show what is still maintained.

example.input: An application with income, debts and time at address, plus a credit bureau report pulled with consent.
example.output: A score, approve or decline, and for a decline the top reasons in plain words, such as "debt is high compared with income", ready for the adverse action notice.

recipes.name: 1. Small lender: explainable scorecard
recipes.when: Credit unions and community banks with no data science team. Cheapest to build and to defend in an exam.
recipes.cost: Open-source software. The cost is a few weeks of modelling on your past loans, then a quarterly review.

recipes.name: 2. Mid-size lender: gradient boosting with reason codes
recipes.when: Fintechs and regional lenders with a validation team.
flow: Reason-code map signed off by compliance
Monthly check against an EBM challenger
recipes.cost: Open-source models. Cash-flow data and decision platforms are sold by contract; none we checked publish a price.

recipes.name: 3. Document-heavy files: AI reads, a normal model scores
recipes.when: Small business, mortgage and other files with many PDFs per application.
flow: Bank statements, pay stubs, tax returns
recipes.cost: Extraction cost about $0.01 to $0.30 per long report with current models in our own benchmark; see the AI document processing guide.

rules.name: Regulation B, 12 CFR 1002.9
rules.what: A lender that declines an applicant must give the specific main reasons within 30 days. Every model needs a clean path from its output to plain-English reasons.

rules.name: CFPB circulars 2022-03 and 2023-03
rules.what: They said complex algorithms are no excuse for vague reasons. The guidance is gone; the rule it explained is not. Don't read the withdrawal as a pass.

rules.name: Fed SR 26-2, model risk guidance
rules.what: Mainly aimed at banks over $30 billion in assets, with generative AI out of scope. Community banks get lighter validation; large banks still document everything.

rules.name: OCC Bulletin 2026-13
rules.what: The OCC adopted the revised model risk guidance and dropped its 1997 credit-scoring exam guide.

rules.name: EU AI Act, Annex III
rules.what: Scoring people's creditworthiness is high-risk; fraud detection is exempt. Plan logging, human oversight and a rights impact assessment now if you lend in the EU.

howToTest: Take two to three years of your booked loans with known outcomes, and hold out the most recent months as the test.
Fit a scorecard, an EBM and LightGBM on the same data, with the same inputs and the same split.
Compare AUC and KS on the held-out months, then turn each model's output into decline reasons and check they stay the same when you refit on a new sample.
Run a bias check across the groups fair-lending exams look at, using fairlearn or your own approval-gap analysis.
Pick the simplest model within a point or two of the best. Extra accuracy that you cannot explain costs more than it earns.

buyVsBuild.buy: Buy a platform when you have no modelling team, need a decision engine anyway, and are happy to use the vendor's models and data partners.
buyVsBuild.build: Build when your own loan history is your edge. Open-source scorecards and boosted models are free, mature and accepted by examiners; the work is data, validation and reason codes.

watchOuts: A credit report's "key factors" list does not count as your decline reasons. Your model must produce its own.
SHAP explains a model; it does not write Regulation B reasons. You need a reason-code map that compliance signs off.
Models trained on past approvals learn past bias. Check approval gaps before launch and every quarter after.
TabPFN's newest weights are non-commercial. Check the licence before production use.
Vendor lift numbers such as more approvals are measured on the vendor's chosen data. Ask for a benchmark on your own loans.
